The Fox and the Tiger: Why Does Borrowed Power Still Command Obedience?
A tiger caught a fox and prepared to eat it.
The fox said:

“You dare not eat me. The Lord of Heaven has appointed me ruler of all the beasts. If you eat me, you will be defying his command. If you don't believe me, let me walk ahead and follow behind. See whether the beasts dare do anything but flee when they see me.”
The tiger agreed.
The fox walked in front, the tiger behind. Seeing them in the distance, the beasts scattered.
The tiger concluded that the beasts really were afraid of the fox.
What he failed to understand was this:
They were afraid of him.
The story became an idiom for frightening others with someone else's power.
But its most interesting question is not simply that the fox “borrowed an aura of authority.”
The beasts really did flee.
And their flight really did save the fox's life.
So is borrowed power real or false?
Judging by the outcome alone, the fox seems genuinely to possess the power to make the beasts give way.
Wherever it walks, the other animals clear a path.
For the moment, the tiger does not eat it, and the beasts do not stop to check its credentials.
This power is no fantasy.
It changes real actions, and it changes who gets to stay alive.
But the fox has not absorbed the power into its own body.
The moment the tiger turns and leaves, the same steps and the same words will very likely stop working.
This is power that exists through a relationship of dependence.
It does not entirely belong to the fox, yet it operates through the fox.
“Not one's own” and “without real effects” are not the same thing.
We often imagine power as something an individual possesses.
Someone is stronger, richer, more knowledgeable, or more famous, so others obey.
But often, people are not responding to the individual standing before them.
They are responding to the position, organization, resources, rules, or possible consequences behind that person.
A notice need not derive its force from the personal standing of whoever delivers it.
A manager's ability to assign work need not mean that the manager is more capable than everyone on the team.
A representative's ability to speak need not mean that the representative is the source of all the power involved.
Power often appears through one person while coming from a larger set of relationships.
That need not be deception.

Living together requires roles and authorization. We cannot meet an entire institution, all its members, or the ultimate decision-maker every time before accepting the validity of a request. Transparent, limited delegation allows common affairs to continue.
The problem is not that power comes from elsewhere.
The questions are:
Has its source been made clear?
Has the person using it presented power temporarily entrusted to them as a status they possess by nature?
The fox's cleverness lies in more than sheltering behind the tiger.
It also devises a test that appears capable of proving its claim.
It says:
If the beasts flee when they see me, that proves I am their ruler.
And the beasts really do flee.
The tiger sees a wholly real event and accepts the wrong explanation.
The test produces the same outcome whichever of two causes is at work:
If the beasts fear the fox, they will flee.
If they fear the tiger, they will also flee.
The fox has chosen evidence that cannot distinguish between the two explanations.
The tiger sees only that the outcome matches the prediction, and assumes the cause has been proved as well.
This is more than gullibility.
It reminds us:
Facts do not automatically tell us why they happened.
Many people obeying an order does not, by itself, prove that they endorse it.
A group remaining silent does not, by itself, prove that no one objects.
Everyone making way for someone does not, by itself, prove that the person has earned their respect.
They may be responding to rules, avoiding a cost, or simply unwilling to face the tiger behind that person.
Reading outward behavior directly as inward approval is one of power's easiest mistakes.
The fable was originally embedded in a political argument.

The king of Chu heard that the northern lords feared Zhao Xixu and asked whether this was true. After telling the story of the fox and the tiger, a minister explained that what the north really feared was the king's army. Zhao Xixu merely wielded that power on his behalf.
The story did not begin, then, as a general mockery of everyone who draws on another's influence.
Its first reminder was to the person holding ultimate power:
Do not mistake people's response to your own power for awe of your agent personally.
That reminder has two sides.
For the agent, borrowed power should not masquerade as personal worth.
For the person granting it, the fact that power works through someone else does not make its consequences none of their concern.
If the beasts flee because of the tiger, the tiger cannot say:
The fox frightened them away. It had nothing to do with me.
The source of power must answer for the effects that power produces.
Nor can the fox, having successfully arranged one procession, declare:
The beasts have acknowledged me as king in their hearts.
Borrowed power is sometimes more stable than personal strength.
An individual may not be powerful, but as long as their position is connected to a functioning institution, their demands will be carried out again and again.
Seeing through the fox's borrowed authority does not therefore mean the fox can be ignored.
If the beasts think only:
The fox itself is weak, so we need not pay attention.
They may still face the tiger a moment later.
An analysis of power cannot stop at exposing the fact:
“There is really nothing much to this person.”
What matters is:
What can they mobilize?
Who will supply consequences for their demands?
Does that support come from explicit authorization, tacit indulgence, or a temporary misunderstanding they have engineered?
If they overstep, will the power behind them still make good on their threats?
These questions determine the reality the beasts face.
A person's individual ability may be small while their role within a relationship is large.
Conversely, even someone highly capable may lack the power to direct shared affairs if no one responds to them.
The fable also includes a participant easily overlooked: the beasts.
They say nothing from beginning to end.
The fox uses their flight to prove its status, and the tiger uses the same flight to confirm the fox's claim.
But not one of them is asked what it actually saw, or why it ran.
Their actions become evidence in someone else's argument.
This resembles the silent participants in many relations of power.
An arrangement goes publicly unchallenged for a long time, so it is taken to have everyone's approval.
People continue to comply, so the rule is taken to be fully legitimate.
But compliance tells us only that the behavior occurred, not that everyone's reasons are the same.
When refusal is costly, obedience is especially difficult to equate with consent.
If we really want to know whom the beasts fear, we cannot leave the explanation of their behavior entirely to the fox and the tiger.
At the very least, the beasts need somewhere to answer without immediately being eaten for it.
Still, the fox is trying to survive.
The tiger has already brought it to the brink of death. It has neither time for a fair discussion nor power equal to the tiger's.
An essay cannot simply stand somewhere safe and condemn it for deception.

In a relationship where the strong can eat the weak at will, a weaker creature escaping through a stronger one's misunderstanding is not quite the same as the powerful using an institution to mislead everyone else.
Circumstances alter our judgment of the means.
But circumstances do not make every means indistinguishable from then on.

This time, the fox merely makes the beasts flee, chiefly deceiving the tiger that intends to eat it. If it later keeps exploiting the tiger's presence to demand resources, impose humiliation, or even present its own orders as Heaven's will, a survival trick will have expanded into a new form of domination.
Borrowing power once to escape danger does not grant every possible use of that power thereafter.
This is where borrowed power most needs limits.
It often begins with a specific authorization, a crisis, or a real need, then gradually forgets why it was given.
The story is usually used to expose the fox.
But it exposes the tiger as well.
The tiger possesses the greatest power in the scene yet fails to understand how that power produces its effects.
He sees the beasts flee without realizing that he is the cause.
Possessing power does not automatically confer an understanding of power.
On the contrary, the greater one's power, the easier it becomes to mistake many different responses for approval.
Others may refrain from arguing simply because they fear the consequences.
They may agree simply because they want access to resources.
They may obey an agent simply because they know who stands behind that agent.
If the holder of power reads all these responses as affection, trust, or recognition of the agent's personal qualities, they are like the tiger: deceived by a phenomenon they themselves have caused.
The fox walks in front, the tiger follows behind.
Who appears to be leading?
The fox.
Who makes the animals along the entire path flee?
The tiger.
Who determines where the procession goes at this moment?
That really is the fox again.
The story rewards rereading precisely because power does not belong neatly to one participant.

The fox lacks the tiger's strength yet briefly directs the tiger. The tiger causes the beasts' fear yet thinks he is merely testing the fox. The beasts respond most realistically of all, yet others use their response to prove an order they never acknowledged.
Borrowed power, then, is not false.
What is false is hiding the relationship of dependence and claiming that every result comes from oneself.
When someone approaches and everyone makes way, the best question may not be:
Is this person really powerful?
It may be:
Are people responding to their reasons, their role, or the silent tiger that has been walking behind them all along?

*Textual basis: the chapter beginning “King Xuan of Jing questioned his ministers” in the Stratagems of the Warring States, “Strategies of Chu I.” In the original, Jiang Yi uses the beasts' flight before the fox and the tiger to explain that the northern lords actually fear the king of Chu's armed forces, not Zhao Xixu personally. This essay distinguishes the person through whom power appears, its source, acts of obedience, and the reasons for those acts.*
